title: Optimize: Cache hit-rate recommendations MVP — outline (types, copy, evidence, success metrics)
content:
Context / why this exists
- We keep getting “cache hit-rate is low / confusing” escalations and we don’t have a consistent way to turn telemetry into next steps.
- This doc is a working outline for the MVP recommendations feed for Optimize.
- Not a full-blown ML system: we’re aiming for a small set of high-signal, explainable heuristics, powered by v2 KV/prefix cache telemetry.

MVP goal (what ‘done’ looks like)
- A customer can open Console → Optimize → Recommendations and see 3–10 “Increase cache hit-rate” items.
- Each item is:
  - understandable in <30 seconds
  - scoped (route/model/region/deployment-mode)
  - includes evidence (what we observed, over what time window)
  - includes an action (what to change) + a suggested validation step
- Internally, CSM/Solutions can point to the same objects to explain “why hit-rate is low” with credible data.

Non-goals (explicit)
- No customer-facing UI polish beyond basic feed + detail drawer.
- No ML clustering pipeline beyond simple bucketing/aggregation.
- No major cache algorithm changes or runtime behavior changes.
- No per-request trace exports into the recommendation (only aggregated evidence; follow ADR-027 cardinality constraints).

Assumptions / dependencies
- Telemetry v2 fields exist and are trustworthy enough:
  - hit/miss/partial classification
  - hit_bytes and miss_bytes or equivalent byte accounting
  - saved_prefill_ms estimate
  - cacheable_prompt_ratio (or a proxy)
  - attribution tags: tenant, route, model, model_version, region, deployment_mode
  - routing fragmentation signals (even if derived): model_variant_count per route, route_count per model, or similar
- Cardinality rules: we will not depend on raw request_id. Any “example prefixes” must be sampled and/or bucketed (hashed prefix bucket id) with strict limits.
- Recommendation generator will run on aggregated rollups (e.g., hourly/daily) in the analytics pipeline.

Recommendation object shape (content requirements)
For each recommendation (feed item) we need:
- Title (short)
- Impact label: High / Medium / Low (heuristic-based)
- Scope:
  - route (optional)
  - model + version (optional)
  - region (optional)
  - deployment_mode (Hosted / Dedicated / Private)
- What we observed (1–3 bullets)
- Why it matters (1–2 sentences)
- What to do (2–5 steps max)
- How to validate (a dashboard query / metric to watch)
- Evidence links:
  - links into Console dashboards (cache hit-rate dashboard drilldown)
  - optional internal: a “telemetry evidence” link (only visible to Redwood staff)
- Suppression controls:
  - dismiss for 7 days / 30 days / permanently
  - “not applicable” reason capture (freeform + tags) — MVP can be minimal

Heuristic recommendation types (MVP candidates)

Type A — Prompt prefix instability (low cacheability)
- Trigger (candidate logic):
  - cacheable_prompt_ratio < threshold (initial guess: < 0.35) AND request volume above minimum
  - AND misses dominated by prefill time (saved_prefill_ms potential is high)
- Typical root causes:
  - timestamps, request ids, user-specific metadata embedded early
  - tool/function call arguments included in the first N tokens
  - dynamic “system prompt” blocks changing across calls
- Evidence to show:
  - cacheable_prompt_ratio over last 7 days, broken down by route
  - top N “prefix buckets” count (or a proxy: prefix diversity index) indicating high variability
  - estimated savings: “If cacheable_prompt_ratio improved to X, we estimate +Y ms saved_prefill_ms/day” (coarse; needs guardrails)
- Customer-facing copy draft:
  - Title: “Normalize the first ~200–400 tokens of your prompt to improve cache hits”
  - What we observed: “Only ~{cacheable_prompt_ratio}% of requests share a stable prompt prefix on route {route}.”
  - Why it matters: “Prefix caching is most effective when the beginning of the prompt stays identical across requests. Instability early in the prompt prevents reuse of prefills.”
  - What to do:
    1) Move dynamic fields (timestamps, ids, user context) after a stable instruction block.
    2) If using tools, keep tool schemas stable and push tool args later.
    3) Consider a two-pass format: stable system + policy prefix, then dynamic user payload.
  - How to validate: “Watch cache_hit_rate and saved_prefill_ms for {route} for 24h after deploying changes.”
- Guardrails:
  - Do not show if cache is disabled / not supported for the model.
  - Do not show if traffic too low (avoid noise + wrong inference).

Type B — Routing fragmentation (requests spread across too many model variants/versions)
- Trigger:
  - route/model fragmentation index > threshold (e.g., top model version < 70% share)
  - AND cache hit-rate below baseline for that route
- Typical root causes:
  - A/B tests or rollouts splitting traffic across versions without considering cache efficacy
  - fallback chains/region spillover producing many model+version combinations
  - customers pinning by “latest” in multiple places
- Evidence:
  - distribution of traffic by model_version for the route
  - hit-rate by model_version (often one version looks healthier)
  - “fragmentation penalty”: hit-rate of combined traffic vs hit-rate within dominant version
- Copy draft:
  - Title: “Reduce model/version fragmentation to increase cache reuse”
  - What we observed: “Traffic for {route} is split across {n} model versions in {region}. The largest version has only {share}% of requests.”
  - Why it matters: “Prefix caches don’t transfer across incompatible model versions. Splitting traffic reduces the chance of cache reuse.”
  - What to do:
    1) Pin {route} to a single model version during peak hours.
    2) If running a rollout, keep the canary population small enough that the primary variant still benefits from caching.
    3) Prefer fewer, longer rollout phases vs frequent small version flips.
  - How to validate: “Compare cache_hit_rate for {route} before/after pinning; also check p95 prefill latency.”
- Notes:
  - Needs careful product positioning: we are not saying “don’t do rollouts” — we’re saying “rollouts change caching economics; plan for it.”

Type C — Route normalization / consolidation (same workload split across many routes)
- Trigger:
  - multiple routes map to same underlying workload (hard) OR “same tenant + same model + similar token profile” across routes
  - simpler MVP: detect “many low-volume routes each with poor hit-rate but collectively large traffic”
- Evidence:
  - top routes by miss_bytes / saved_prefill_ms opportunity
  - combined traffic of top K related routes (by name prefix? path prefix?)
- Copy draft:
  - Title: “Consolidate similar traffic into fewer routes for better caching”
  - What we observed: “{tenant} has {n} routes each under {qps} QPS, with low cache reuse.”
  - Why it matters: “Caches warm faster with higher reuse on a single route/model combination. Fragmentation can keep caches cold.”
  - What to do:
    1) Merge equivalent prompts behind a single route when possible.
    2) Keep route-level prompt templates consistent.
    3) If you need multiple routes, consider pinning them to the same model+version and prompt prefix.

Type D — Cache policy mismatch (TTL/evictions / capacity pressure)
- Trigger:
  - high eviction rate OR hit-rate stable but hit_bytes low + many inserts (depends on spec availability)
  - if we have “evict_reason=capacity” counts, use that
- Evidence:
  - evictions over time; hit-rate falling during bursts
  - if available: cache utilization proxy
- Copy draft:
  - Title: “Adjust cache policy to reduce evictions during peak traffic”
  - What we observed: “Cache evictions spike during peak hours and hit-rate drops by {delta}%.”
  - What to do:
    1) Increase cache capacity (Dedicated: reserved memory / GPU pool sizing; Hosted: request support if applicable).
    2) Tune TTL to match reuse patterns (shorter TTL if pollution, longer TTL if stable repeats).
    3) Consider separate routing tiers for highly-cacheable traffic.
- Caveat:
  - This risks becoming deployment-mode specific quickly. For MVP, keep it to a small number of supported knobs + “talk to us” CTA where necessary.

Type E — Streaming retries / partial-prefill skew (data quality + fixable config)
- Trigger:
  - mismatch between measured hit-rate and observed latency savings (if we can detect)
  - high partial rate, high retry rate, or known “streaming retry” signatures
- Evidence:
  - partial rate, retry counters; saved_prefill_ms not tracking hit-rate
- Copy draft (customer-safe):
  - Title: “Check for retries/partial prefills reducing effective cache savings”
  - What we observed: “A high share of requests are classified as partial hits; effective savings are lower than expected.”
  - What to do:
    1) Ensure client retry behavior is configured to avoid duplicating prefill work.
    2) Validate streaming settings and timeouts.
    3) If the issue persists, share request samples with support (we’ll provide what fields).
- Note:
  - This may be better as an internal-facing “data quality” recommendation first, depending on sensitivity.

Recommendation ranking (MVP)
- Rank by “estimated impact” rather than just “lowest hit-rate”.
- Proposed simple score (rough):
  - score = (miss_prefill_ms * traffic_weight) * confidence
  - where confidence penalizes low volume, high sampling, unstable attribution
- Ensure we don’t spam: max 2 recommendations per route, and max 10 overall.

Evidence requirements (minimum bar for MVP)
- Every recommendation must include:
  - time window (default 7 days, with ability to change later)
  - the key metric deltas that triggered it (e.g., cache_hit_rate, cacheable_prompt_ratio, fragmentation share)
  - a comparison baseline (account-level baseline or previous week)
- Every recommendation should include at least 1 “where to look” dashboard deep link.
- No raw prompt text is shown. If we ever show “example prefix buckets” they must be:
  - hashed/bucket ids + counts only
  - sampled and capped (e.g., top 20 buckets)

Copy / UX details (draft)
- Category name in feed: “Increase cache hit-rate” (future: split into “Performance” and “Cost”, but for MVP keep one)
- Impact label text:
  - High: “High potential savings”
  - Medium: “Potential savings”
  - Low: “Small improvement”
- CTA button copy options:
  - “View evidence” (opens metrics)
  - “How to fix” (opens steps; can combine with evidence in same drawer)
- Validation step should be explicit (avoid ‘trust us’):
  - “After deploying, watch saved_prefill_ms and cache_hit_rate on {route} for 24h.”

Guardrails / don’t embarrass ourselves
- Don’t recommend prompt normalization if cacheable_prompt_ratio already high.
- Don’t recommend “pin to one model version” if customer is in an active rollout (Rollouts product) unless we can phrase it as “adjust rollout to preserve caching.”
- Don’t recommend “increase cache capacity” for Hosted in a way that implies the customer controls it; phrase as “contact support / upgrade tier” where appropriate.
- Show confidence when we have it (and a “why we’re suggesting this” explainer).

Success metrics (MVP)
Product metrics (leading)
- Recommendation view rate: % of active tenants who view at least one cache recommendation per week.
- CTR: % who click “View evidence” / expand details.
- Dismissal rate and reasons (esp. “not applicable”).
- Time-to-first-action proxy: click + subsequent telemetry improvement event.

Outcome metrics (lagging; directionally measured)
- Improvement in cache_hit_rate (route-level) for tenants exposed to recs vs control (if we can do simple holdback).
- Improvement in saved_prefill_ms/day (more meaningful than raw hit-rate).
- Reduction in p95 prefill latency for targeted routes.
- Cost proxy: reduction in prefill GPU time per 1k requests (needs careful interpretation).

Internal success
- Support: reduce number of cache-metric confusion tickets / time-to-triage.
- Solutions: ability to use the recommendation + evidence in customer calls (qualitative feedback).

Open questions / TODO
- Threshold tuning:
  - what is “low cacheable_prompt_ratio” by deployment mode and model family?
  - how to normalize across different prompt length distributions?
- How do we compute “prefix diversity index” without leaking sensitive data?
  - option: hashed prefix bucket counts using first N tokens (N configurable), with strict sampling.
- Evidence links: what’s the stable deep link format for the cache dashboards?
- Suppression semantics:
  - if dismissed permanently, do we ever re-surface? (maybe if score increases 5x)
- Private deployments:
  - are we generating recs in-customer environment or in our control plane? (likely varies; keep MVP to Hosted + Dedicated first)

Next steps (as of last edit)
- Align on the final MVP recommendation set (pick 3 types to start):
  - A (prompt prefix instability)
  - B (version fragmentation)
  - D (evictions/policy mismatch) OR C (route fragmentation) depending on telemetry readiness
- Confirm evidence fields available from Telemetry v2 rollups with Logan/Nadia.
- Finalize API contract in PM-912 and ensure backend storage supports:
  - score, title, body, evidence blobs (as references), suppression status
- Define rollout gating:
  - behind feature flag, start with internal tenants and a small set of design partners
  - ensure we can turn off generation independently from display
